translations.text: A discourse by the same, our blessed father John, abbot of Sinai, addressed to the shepherd and superior,
which he gave, together with these other chapters mentioned earlier, to John, abbot of Raithu, who had asked him
to write down for him the teachings of the monastic life. In this book of the earth I, the last of all, have written to you, O God-clad one;
but in that heavenly one, I believe, you were before all in honor, in that divine book of inscription, if that saying is true that those who are [first?] in mind are [first?] in honor.
CHAPTER 1. The true shepherd is he who is able, by his purity,
and by his own zeal and prayer, to seek out and raise up the lost rational sheep. The true ship's master is he who has received power from God invisibly,
and from his own labors, to bring the ship up not only from the waves but even from the abyss. The physician is he
whose soul and body are whole and unharmed, and who needs no medicine from anyone. The teacher is he who has received the spiritual book of understanding,
written by the finger of God, which is the power of his radiance, and who needs nothing from other books.
Shameful is the teacher who teaches only from writings, and the painter who cannot depict anything without a model. Those whom you wish to teach on earth,
teach from heaven, and teach others by the example of your deeds. Do not forget the speaker who says: Not for the sake of men,
nor through men do I teach the teaching; for by earthly things you will not heal the sickness of the soul. A good ship's master brings the ship to safety,
and a good shepherd keeps alive and heals the sick sheep. However much those sheep follow the shepherd obediently and without breaking away,
so much will that shepherd give an account for them to their Lord. Let the shepherd strike with the word, as with a thrown stone, the sheep that have lagged behind through sloth or gluttony,
for this too is the mark of a good shepherd. When the sheep, from the heat and labor of this flesh, begin to fall asleep in spirit,
then the shepherd must all the more look to heaven and keep watch for them, for in that time of heat the beast has destroyed many.
And now, just as we see the habit among sheep, that in the time of heat they bend their heads toward the ground, so too humility toward one another befits us,
for it is written that in the darkness of night, when beasts approach the flock, then they tie the dog at the night fire, immovable,
so that it may keep them away. And you, in that darkness of the passions, set that mind of yours, the slayer of beasts, as guardian of that spiritual flock.
CHAPTER 2. This too our good God made a habit of nature: that the sick, when they see a physician, rejoice, even if he does them no healing at all. You too, O marvelous one, acquire
medicines to apply to wounds, plaster, and agents that dry wounds, and medicines to drink, and eye salves;
and those that set broken limbs; and cleansers of [?]; and those that stop foul odors;
lancets for opening veins, and cauterizing instruments, and ointments for wounds; and sleeping drugs, and knives for cutting, and bandages for what is crushed;
But if we are empty of all this, how shall we show the art of healing? For the rewards are not for words but for deeds. A plaster is
the healing of visible, bodily passions. A potion to drink is the healing of inner passions and the emptying out of invisible filth. A blood-staunching medicine is
reviling and contempt, which pains the heart and heals it, and dries up the swelling and rottenness of pride. An eye-salve, for the troubled eyes of the soul, is
a reproof that cleanses from anger. A lancet for opening a vein is the swift emptying out of invisible stench. The true vein-opener is swift and harsh humiliation,
for the healing of those who are sick. A cleansing sponge is, after the cutting of the vein,
the relief of the sick man through the sweet and gentle words of the shepherd and physician. Cautery is a canon imposed for some length of time, for the repentance and life of the sick man.
An ointment after the burning is the comforting of the sick man, by word or by bodily consolation. A sleeping-draught is bearing the burden, the burden of the obedient one,
so that through obedience it may bring him rest, and sleepless sleep, and the good blindness of not seeing his own virtues. A bandage, for those released from haughtiness, is
strengthening by the remembrance of death. And at the end of all is the sword: the sentence and the cutting off of a spiritual limb that is rotten
and incurable, so that it may not pass on its disease and [?] to others as well. Among physicians, blessed is that medicine which makes foul odor imperceptible,
so that whoever has it no longer smells the stench; and likewise among superiors, blessed is dispassion,
for when those physicians do not smell the odor of the stench, they readily approach the healing of every wound;
and when these superiors acquire dispassion, they are able to raise up every dead soul.
This too is required of the superior, along with his other tasks: that he honor each according to his worth and show love,
lest, as Jacob did, he harm both the beloved one and the others with him.
This happens to those whose spiritual senses have not been fully trained to distinguish the good, the bad, and the intermediate.
Chapter 3. It is a shame for a shepherd if he prays that his disciples be given what he himself has not acquired. Just as those who see the face of the king
and make him their friend, and all his nobles as well, are thereafter able, even on behalf of those unknown to the king,

or even on behalf of their own enemies, to intercede if they wish, and to bring them before the king, so also understand concerning the saints; for one feels shame before beloved friends, before those who love him.
It is good that we acquire those invisible powers as friends, for no one else is so able to help us toward virtue.
One of the lovers of God told me that always, but especially on the feasts of the Lord, God bestows gifts and graces on his own servants.
Chapter 4. The physician must have the passions wholly destroyed in him, so that he may thus be able, at the time when it is fitting, to feign one of the passions, and especially anger;
for if he has [? not] wholly wiped them from his soul, he cannot feign them without passion. I saw a horse that had not yet been fully tamed,
And therefore, as long as the rider sitting on it held the reins firmly in his hands, it went along quietly; but at a certain moment he slackened the reins a little,
and it was harmed and harmed him as well. This parable applies above all to two demons; let whoever wishes to understand it, understand.
Chapter 5. The physician will recognize the wisdom given to him by God when he is able to heal passions that many others could not cure.
That teacher is no marvel who through instruction has made wise boys who were already well taught; but he who has the untaught
and dull of mind instructed and made perfect is. The skill of charioteers shows itself when they master an untried horse
and bring those horses safely through. If eyes have been given to you to foresee the waves for those who are in the boat,
to foresee the waves for those who are in the boat, tell them beforehand; if not, you are the cause of their drowning,
since the guidance of the sailors has been entrusted to you. I have seen physicians who did not inform the sick beforehand of the causes of the disease,
and thereby brought great ruin and toil on both the sick person and themselves. As much as the superior sees the disciples' faith in him,
so much let him guard himself with all caution, in deeds and in words, so as to give offense to no one, since all look to him
as to their image and pattern and the rule of their conduct. Love for the flock reveals the true shepherd, for it was out of love that the good shepherd was crucified.
Chapter 6. Speak all your words with understanding, and may it nowhere harm you. Afflict the sick person for a short time,
so that the sickness may not be prolonged, or lest he die altogether because of that harmful silence of yours. Many, because of the silence of the pilot,
thought they were going along well, until their boat struck a rock and was shattered. Let us listen to the great Paul, how he writes to Timothy
and tells him: Reprove, rebuke, and comfort, in season and out of season. And in season, as I think, is when those reproved bear it patiently;
and out of season is when they are inflamed and distressed by it; for springs too, even if no one is thirsty, do not cease to send up water. Some superiors have a bashful nature,
and they do not reprove where the disciples need it; these I charge not to cease carrying out a teacher's works on the disciples,
so that they may not be harmed themselves and harm them as well. Let us listen to that divine voice which says: Cut it off, so that it may not lead the land astray as well;
and again it says: Let wickedness be removed from among you; and again it says: Do not pray to me for this people;
and likewise again, concerning Saul, he said to Samuel: Why are you grieving for Saul, when I have cast him away from me?
All this the shepherd must know: in what matters, and when, and how it ought to be done;
for nothing is truer than God. Whoever is not ashamed when you rebuke him in private will not be ashamed even if you rebuke him before the multitude;
for he has taken on the habit of evil and has come to hate his own life.
Chapter 7. I have seen good sick people who knew their own timidity and impatience, and even though the physicians did not wish to bind them and treat them in that way;
Rather, they willingly begged the physician to heal them by force and against their will;
for the spirit was zealous for the eternal hope, but the flesh was weak because of their former habits.
When I saw them, I counseled the physicians to listen to them. The superior should not say to all who come to him
that the gate is narrow and hard, nor should he say to all that the yoke is sweet and the burden small;
rather, he should apply the medicine as is fitting for each one. Those who were weighed down and weakened by grievous sins he should tell the second,
those who were inclined to despair. And again, for those whose mind is inclined to loftiness and pride,
the first is good. Certain people wished to travel on a long road, and they asked those who knew the road, and these told them that it is easy and level.
Therefore, on their word, they began to walk carelessly, and halfway along the road they gave up or else turned back, because they were unprepared for its struggles.
And understand the opposite in the same way. Where the desire for God has drawn near to the heart, there severity of words could not frighten;
where fear of Gehenna has entered, there taking on all labors has become easy;
and where hope of the Kingdom is recognized, there is contempt for everything on earth. A good commander must
know the strength and courage of each one of his host, for there may be among his host some who fight in the front line
and some who fight alone, who ought to sit in stillness. The master of a ship cannot save the ship by himself, without the help of the sailors,
nor can a physician heal a sick person, unless the sick person shows him his wound and begs him to heal that wound.
Those who were ashamed before the physician let their wounds rot, and many even died altogether.
Chapter 8. When the sheep are grazing, let the shepherd not cease piping the word, and especially when they are about to fall asleep;
for the wolf fears nothing so much as the shepherd's pipe. The shepherd should neither always humble himself without understanding, nor always exalt himself foolishly,
since he sees that Paul, the great apostle, conducted himself fittingly in both of these. Many times the Lord has held back the eyes of obedient newcomers,
so that they would not see the shortcomings of their teacher; but some superiors have revealed these to them
and brought harm upon them. I saw a superior who, out of his great humility, would consult his children when he intended to do something;
and I saw another, who foolishly revealed his own blindness and consulted them on certain matters with reproach. I saw people subject to the passions
who began to serve as superiors while still subject to the passions, and little by little they became ashamed before their disciples and cut off their passions.

This, as I think, was accomplished in them by the reward for those who were saved through them, and the work they began while subject to the passions became for them the cause of freedom from the passions.
Chapter 9. Let us take care lest we scatter at sea what was gained in the harbor. This saying is understood by those
who are as yet unshepherded in the good and who enter into tumults and bodily cares. It is truly a great thing, with long-suffering and courage,
patience in the heat of stillness and in its weariness, and that he not seek to go outside the cell or after amusements,
as faint-hearted sailors do, who swim in the water in the time of calm.
But far higher still is not to fear disturbances and tumults, but to remain among them with an untroubled and unmoved heart, being in body with people and in mind with God.
Chapter 10. This too, O wondrous one, must be examined: who comes condemned to this fearful and true tribunal of ours,
or who, being innocent, hastens to the service and slavery of God; for the departures of these two are opposed to one another,
and they need separate ways of life. Before all else, question the one who has come, on his own, about what his deeds are,
so that two benefits may come from the confession: that he may be ashamed because of that confession and always stay far from boldness,
and that he may know what burdens of his we have become guarantor for, and may be moved to love. Do not be ignorant of this, O honored one!
just as you are indeed not ignorant, far be it, that God judges those who have sinned according to their place and mind
and upbringing; so you too should do, for there is great difference in matters of sin. Many times the weaker person is also lower in mind;
for this reason he also deserves to be punished more lightly by those spiritual judges, and the opposite of this is evident.
Chapter 11. There is no peace if a lion shepherds sheep;
and it is not without error if one who is subject to passions is the leader of others subject to passions. A fox among hens is an ugly thing, and anger in leaders is an ugly thing;
for the one eats hens, while the other harms rational souls. Take care: do not be, beyond measure, an investigator of small matters,
so that in this way you may become like God. Have God as the guide of all your affairs, those of the heart and the outward ones, and do not do your own will in anything,
but his, so that you too may become free of care, when you have entrusted everything to him and act at his nod. This must be examined among us:
whether it is because of the faith of those who come to us, and not from our own diligence, that grace has come upon us from God,
for many who were subject to passions have also worked miracles in this way. If many will say to the Lord on that day, "Lord, did we not prophesy in your name?",
then this point stated above is in no way incredible. Whoever has truly obtained mercy from God is able to do good to the weak without being noticed, and in this way he does two great goods:
first, in that he keeps himself unharmed by the venom of glory; and second, in that he moves those who have received mercy to offer thanks to God alone.
Chapter 12. Those who walk the road strongly, set strong, perfect and firm medicine before them; but those who are still infants in mind, give them milk,
as to infants, for there is a time for each food. One and the same food brings eagerness to some and faint-heartedness to others;
for this reason it is right that we sow the seed according to the time, the person and the measure. Some have reckoned the work of guiding souls as nothing;
and they foolishly undertook the guidance of souls, and they had great wealth, yet they departed from here empty of all of it,
for through that guidance they distributed it to others. Just as there are true sons, and others born of a second wife, and others abandoned,
and others born of a maidservant, so too spiritual direction takes various forms. True direction is the giving of one's soul, wholly, for the soul of one's neighbor;
another kind is the bearing of past sins only; and another is the bearing only of the weight of the tasks he commands,
because of a lack of dispassion and spiritual power. Even in that perfect direction, in proportion to their surrender of their own will,
we bear the judgment. A faithful son is recognized when his father is not with him. Let the superior discipline
those who answer him back in front of people and in the presence of great persons, and let him impose a heavy penance on them, so that fear may come upon others also because of them,
even though it pains them sorely and they are embittered by that rebuke, for the benefit of many is better than the harm of one. There are some
who out of love bear the burdens of others even beyond their own strength, because of the saying that says: Greater
love than this no one has, and what follows it. And there are others who have received from God the strength for the burden,
and yet do not do this, so as to save a brother and bear the weight for the sake of his life.
But I reproach them as strangers to love, and they seem pitiable to me;
but first, concerning the former, I have found the writing that says that whoever brings forth the precious from the impure shall be as my mouth;
and again the one that says: As you have done to him, so may it be done to you. Understand this also: that often a superior's sin in thought is judged more grievous than a disciple's sin in deed;
for a soldier's sin is lighter than a general's evil counsel. Teach your disciples not to recall carnal sins in detail, how they were committed,
but to recall all other sins night and day, how they were committed. Teach them to be entirely innocent toward one another, but wise and full of stratagems against the demons,
and in this offer yourself as a model. Let not even the love of your flock for one another be hidden from you, for it is a stratagem of wolves
to slacken even the zealous through the slack. Do not be negligent in praying for the negligent, not that they may be shown mercy, for this is impossible as long as they do not help you,
but pray for this: that God may bring them to zeal. Let the weak not go to eat with heretics, as is written by the fathers; but the strong,
if they wish to go and even to eat, let them go for the glory of the Lord. Do not plead ignorance as an excuse, for whoever does not know and does what deserves a beating will be beaten, which
means: he learned. CHAPTER 13. Fear of death is a shameful thing in a shepherd, since even this obedience is fearlessness of death;
does not the office of superior, then, have much greater need of fearlessness of death? Seek out, O blessed one,
the virtues without which, and without purity of soul and body, the Lord is not seen, and teach these to your children before all else;
and keep them away from the sight of all women and harmful persons. According to the strength and measure of each of those under us, let us arrange their tasks,
For no one ought to leave the harbor. Before due testing, let us lay hands on no one, neither for a bribe nor for noble birth,
for such men are liable to punishment, lest they be unable to bear the heat and toil of the monastic life and return to the world, and those who laid hands on them
will not be blameless when they answer before God. There is a certain kind of champion of God whose own tears and labors no longer serve for himself,
but he employs them on behalf of others, without shame before God. Do not grow weary of making holy souls and bodies that have been defiled,
so that you may receive from God a crown not only for your own soul and your neighbor's, but also for other souls,
when you have become a model of good for others and God is glorified through you, and you may boldly ask him for your reward. I saw a certain weak brother
who by faith purified the weakness of another weak man, when he used a praiseworthy shamelessness on his behalf toward God
and laid down his own soul for that man's soul, yet with humility, and through healing him he healed himself as well;
and I saw another who did the same with pride, and he heard with wrath:
"Physician, first heal yourself." There is a withdrawal from what is good that is higher still and is for the sake of good, as with that man who was even kept back from martyrdom,
not because he was afraid, but for the sake of the others who were profiting from him and being enlightened. There is a man who for the honor of another gives himself over to contempt,
and he is reckoned by others a lover of pleasure and a servant, yet he is genuine. If one who has a profitable word and does not give it ungrudgingly
will not escape guilt, then how much guilt, beloved, will come upon the one who is able to help by deeds as well and does not help? Deliver, you who have been delivered by God;
save, you who have been saved; rescue those going to death, and ransom those being killed by the devil,
for this is a work surpassing every work and contemplation of men and angels. He who, by the purity given to him by God,
cleanses the defilements of another shows himself a helper of the bodiless powers;
for he offers spotless sacrifices to God, and this is the work of the angels, for they offer him as gifts
all the souls that are around him. Nothing so shows toward us the love for mankind and the goodness of our Creator
as this, that he left the ninety-nine and came to seek the one sheep
that had strayed. You too, O blessed one, take care, and show all your zeal and love and fervor and striving and supplication to God on behalf of the one who has strayed and been broken, for
where sicknesses and wounds are great, there without doubt great rewards too are given. Let us examine and understand
that a superior need not always judge justly, because of weakness. I saw two litigants before a most wise judge,
and he acquitted the unjust one as being weak, but disappointed the just one as being strong, so that he might not cause a greater division by just judgment,
and privately he told each one his own case, and especially the one who was weak. A green field is good for all sheep;
But the teaching and remembrance of death is good and profitable for all rational sheep. Insult and shame the weak in the presence of the long-suffering,
so that with the medicine of one you may heal the wound of another, and may teach those long-suffering ones greater patience. Nowhere has God exposed anyone's confession,
so that he might not make those who confess stumble through that exposure, and they then fall incurably sick. Even if you have the grace of foreknowledge,
let us not tell those who have erred what we know beforehand, but rather let us bring them to confession by skillful means,
so that through that confession they too may find relief from that error of theirs. After confession, more than before,
let us give them boldness toward us, for in this way they advance greatly in faith and love toward us,
and again it is fitting for us to teach them to have fear toward us;
and we in turn should show them a model of humility. See that your immeasurable humility does not
heap coals of fire on the head of your children. In everything you are bound to be patient,

except for the disobedience of those under your command. Consider whether there may be trees in that vineyard of yours that only lead the ground astray, and whether they may be able to bear fruit in another place;
let us not be negligent in uprooting these with love and planting them in another place. Perhaps a superior may be able, even in places close to the world,
to practice virtue without stumbling, but let him take care for those who are with him, and if he wishes to be there, let him not receive brothers who are afflicted by passions,
for not every refusal to receive is harmful. If the physician has spiritual stillness, bodily stillness is not greatly needed by him in his healing of the sick,
but if he does not have the former, let him make use of the latter. No gift is offered by us to God so well
as bringing rational souls to him through repentance. The whole world is not worth one soul, for the one passes away, while the other remains for you forever.
Chapter 14. Therefore, blessed one, do not call blessed those who offer riches,
but those who offer rational sheep to Christ. Let your sacrifice be spotless, or else what profit will it be to you? Just as it was ordained that the Son of Man be handed over,
but woe to him by whom he is handed over, so likewise understand the opposite of this: that salvation was ordained for all who are zealous,
but the reward belongs to him through whom their life came about. After God, we also need great spiritual strength [?: the text has 'woman', probably an error for 'strength'], O
holy father, so that those whom we have undertaken to lead into the Holy of Holies and to offer at the altar of Christ,
while they are before the doors of the entrance, if we see them hard pressed by that harmful multitude,

let us hold them by their hands like infants and free them from that harm of thoughts. But if they are very infantile and weak, let us carry them on our shoulders and lift them up until they pass through that narrow and difficult gate,
for all the pressing and crowding happens there; for this reason the prophet said: This is a great labor before me,
that I might only just enter the sanctuary of God. It has been said by us in the chapters above, O father of fathers, concerning that father of fathers and teacher of teachers,
what sort of man he was in heavenly wisdom: adorned in every way, fitting in his reproof, holy, merciful, forgiving, radiant;
and the best thing of all in him was this: if he saw that anyone wished to be saved, he would devote greater diligence to him;
and again, when he saw any who held to their own will and to the love of some thing, he would strive so hard to cut off that will that all of them would flee from having anything
according to their own will. And that blessed man also used to say this: that it is better to expel from the monastery
than to permit disciples to have their own will, for he who expels often humbles the one expelled.
But he who indulges someone's will, as though out of mercy, will be such that at the hour of death they will pitiably curse him,
for he led them astray and did them no good. That great man also had this custom: after the evening office he would sit upon a seat, in body on one of wood,
and in spirit on one of graces, like a king, and that good assembly would stand around him like wise bees;
and they listened to his words as to the words of God, and obeyed his commands.
To one he would order fifty psalms, to another seventy psalms, and to another a hundred, to be said before sleeping,
and to another he would likewise order genuflections; to another he would allow sleep in a sitting position; for another he would appoint a time for reading books;
and another he would order to pray and to stand at an appointed time. And he had appointed two brothers as overseers, so that by day they would restrain them from idle talk,
and by night again from idle wakefulness or from conversing with one another. And again at table too that great man had established a rule for each one,
for the food was not the same for all, but a rule was set for each; and that good steward would order one to take dry bread and water,
and others he would comfort more abundantly. And this was the marvel: that they received everything without murmuring, as from the mouth of God.
And that great man had, below, that place of the prison of which we spoke, and above that great monastery, again another lavra, into which
that strong and perfect man would send the strong to live in seclusion. Do not, I beg you, allow the straightforward to become crooked;
but rather, if you are able, bring the crooked to straightness. He who has become entirely dispassionate is able to carry out judgment well
and as is proper, for a lack of dispassion strikes the heart of the judge
and does not allow judgment to be carried out fittingly. Leave to your children, before all else, the inheritance of the true faith,
so that not only your children but also your grandchildren may be offered to the Lord in orthodoxy. Ardent and stiff-necked youths
do not spare from chastisement, so that at the hour of death they may glorify you. In this too let that great Moses be a model for you, O
most wise one, for those subject to him could not be freed from Pharaoh until they had eaten unleavened bread. The unleavened bread is this:
that a disciple should have no indulgence of his own will, for the will raises a man up, while unleavened bread is always low;
and by the wild herb [?] let us understand the severity of the teacher's reproof and shaming, and the narrowness of fasting.
which brings bitterness to the flesh, yet they are sweet to the soul, more than honey from the comb. But I, O father of fathers, who write this to you, tremble at the word which says:
"You who teach another, why do you not become a teacher of yourself?" But now I have said this much, and I will halt the course of my speech.
Chapter 15. The heart which through holiness has been joined to God
has no need of another's word for teaching, for it has that beginningless Word as teacher and guide and enlightener of that blessed one, as is your holiness,
whom I know not by mere word, but have tested by deed: that all-holy mind of yours, slayer of those evil beasts,
by your meekness and humility, like that great lawgiver Moses, in whose footsteps you have followed, and you have almost surpassed even him in the grace of holiness and virginity,
by which, more than by anything else, it is possible to draw near to God, the holy and incorruptible one, who is the bestower of incorruption,
and who raises those who strive from earth to heaven. For this reason you too, lifted up as if by a chariot of fire, like that great Elijah,
not only killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand of humility, but you also went up the mountain and saw God by a thorny and harsh
and hard-to-bear way of life. And you heard the voice of God and saw his light, and you took from the feet of the soul the sandals, which are the matter of the passions;
and you seized by the tail him who, from among the angels, became a serpent, and you cast him down into the cave of the underworld;
and you became victor over Pharaoh, that lofty and arrogant one, and you struck the Egyptians,
and you slew their firstborn, which is a great wonder. For this reason too the Lord entrusted to you the leadership of the brethren,
whom you delivered, O blessed one, from Pharaoh and from that evil brick, and you gave them a pillar of fire
and of divine cloud, the quencher of every furnace of the passions. And not only this, but this purple and fire-
colored sea you parted for them, in which many of us have drowned, and you showed them victorious by the rod of your shepherding, and you utterly drowned all their pursuers;
and besides this, that Amalek of pride as well, who attacks after the crossing of the sea, you slew by the raising of your hands,
between action and contemplation, for the sake of the people entrusted to you by God, and you became victor over the gentiles,
and you led your people up to the mountain of dispassion. You appointed priests for them and taught the circumcision of dispassion,
without which God is not seen, unless there is a circumcision of the passions and the coming of holiness;
and you went up to the height and cut through all the darkness of ignorance, and you drew near to a light far exceeding that of the thornbush, and you were made worthy of the divine voice,
and you were made worthy of vision and prophecy, and you saw God from the back, that is, that eternal light which is to come,
and you heard the voice saying, "No man shall see my face." And then you went down into the depth of humility at Horeb,
and you had with you those tablets of understanding written by God, and the face of both soul and body was glorified.
[?] what shall I say about the calf? O that deed! O, that breaking of the tablets! And then when [?] you held the hand of the people;
And you passed through that desert and quenched the flame of thirst, and you bestowed those springs of tears by means of the wood,
which is the crucifixion of the flesh with its passions and desires; and you burned up those evil gentiles with fire from God;
and you came to the Jordan, for nothing prevents us from leaving out some small part of that ancient figure,
for you parted that great river and gave over the lower waters to the sea of salt and death; and those other waters, the waters of love,
you dammed up above, before the eyes of those spiritual Israelites. And you commanded that the twelve stones be taken up, or rather the number of the apostles, and by them you built;
or else you signified the victory over the eight passions and the acquisition of the four great virtues; and you left that dead and fruitless sea entirely behind your back,
and you came to the city of Jericho, and you blew the trumpet of prayer through the seven-day period of the times of this world,
and you threw down those walls and conquered, until you too cried out to that immaterial Helper that the sword of the enemy has utterly failed, and that you have thrown down the walls of my passions.
But I will say something greater still: you went up to Jerusalem, which is the vision of perfect peace, and you saw Christ, the God of peace, and with him you struggled,
like a good soldier; with him you were crucified in the flesh with its passions and desires, and you too were made by God a god to Pharaoh
and to every opposing power; and you were buried with Christ, and with him you descended into those depths of theology,
and you received ointment from those friends, the virtues, and so you rose, for what prevents me from speaking of each thing in turn? You rose on the third day,
that is, after the defeat of those three tyrants: gluttony, love of money, and arrogance;
and even more, after the purification of soul, body, and mind from desire, anger, and evil thoughts. And you ascended the Mount of Olives, that mountain of which the holy one said:
"The high mountains are for the deer," that is, for the souls that slay the passions. For it is proper to be brief, and not to speak wisdom at length
to one full of wisdom, and moreover one better informed than all of us, for you ascended that mountain of which Scripture said
that it is for those who slay the passions. After this, then, you too ascended and lifted your eyes to heaven, for let me bring the course of the discourse back again to the discourse:
Bless us, your disciples, and consider that ladder of the virtues set before you, whose foundation you laid by the grace of God given to you,
like a wise master builder, and moreover bring it to completion. Although in the depth of your humility you have compelled this poor and unlearned mouth of ours to be opened to your people,
and this is no wonder, for Moses too called himself weak of voice and slow of tongue, but he had Aaron with him, who spoke well;
but as for you, blessed one, I do not know why you have come to a spring that is dried up and filled with the frogs of Egypt, and worse still, with the coals of Egypt. And
since it is not right to leave the figure and parable of your ascent unfinished, I therefore return to my earlier discourse;
for you ascended that holy mountain, and lifted your eyes to heaven, and set your feet on the ladder of the virtues; you ascended and were exalted;

And you took flight and rose up with crying aloud, and you became victor over the enemies, and you wounded them, and you went on ahead leading the way, and still more, even now, you always lead all of us,
for you have ascended to the top of that holy ladder of the virtues and have been united to love;
and love is God, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and unto the ages of ages. Amen.
